The IPL trade market is already witnessing major shake-ups ahead of the 2027 season, with Hardik Pandya and Arshdeep Singh set to swap franchises and Rishabh Pant and Kuldeep Yadav also heading in opposite directions.It follows a busy 2026 trade window, headlined by the high-profile deal that sent Sanju Samson to Chennai Super Kings, with Ravindra Jadeja and Sam Curran moving to Rajasthan Royals.But big trades are nothing new in the IPL. The story goes back to 2009, when Zaheer Khan moved from Royal Challengers Bangalore to Mumbai Indians in a swap involving Robin Uthappa. Since then, the league has seen some surprising deals - Shikhar Dhawan's three-player exchange in 2018, Ravichandran Ashwin's move from Kings XI Punjab to Delhi Capitals in 2020, and Mayank Markande being traded twice in the same window.Some moves have proved masterstrokes, like Trent Boult's arrival at Mumbai Indians, while others have failed to deliver. Here is a look at the biggest IPL trades and the deals that have shaped the league's history.The IPL has seen some big names switch sides over the years, and a few of those deals have had a major impact on the teams involved. The Hardik Pandya-Arshdeep Singh swap is the latest to grab attention, with two India internationals heading in opposite directions ahead of the 2027 season. The Sanju Samson-Ravindra Jadeja-Sam Curran deal is another big one, while Hardik's return to Mumbai Indians and Cameron Green's move to RCB also stand out.There have been several other interesting moves, including Rishabh Pant's return to Delhi, Shikhar Dhawan's multi-player deal and Ashwin's move to Delhi. We also go back to some of the early swaps involving Zaheer Khan, Robin Uthappa, Ross Taylor and Ashish Nehra.Apart from the -Arshdeep, Pant-Kuldeep swap, The window has also seen T Natarajan returning to Sunrisers Hyderabad from Delhi, while Zeeshan Ansari has moved to the Capitals. Chennai Super Kings and SRH have completed a four-player exchange involving Liam Livingstone, Jack Edwards, Khaleel Ahmed and Nathan Ellis, with Livingstone's fee revised to Rs 6 crore.The 2026 trading window was headlined by a three-player exchange between Rajasthan Royals and Chennai Super Kings. Sanju Samson moved to CSK, while Ravindra Jadeja and Sam Curran joined Rajasthan. Samson retained his Rs 18 crore fee, while Jadeja's fee was revised to Rs 14 crore and Curran retained Rs 2.4 crore.Hardik Pandya's return to Mumbai Indians was the headline move ahead of the 2024 season. Hardik joined Mumbai from Gujarat Titans at his existing league fee of Rs 15 crore, returning to the franchise where he began his IPL career after leading Gujarat to a title and a runners-up finish. Cameron Green moved from Mumbai to Royal Challengers Bangalore at his existing fee of Rs 17.5 crore.Kolkata Knight Riders were among the most active franchises ahead of the 2023 season, bringing in Lockie Ferguson and Rahmanullah Gurbaz from Gujarat Titans, along with Shardul Thakur from Delhi CapitalsThe trading activity ahead of the 2021 season featured three notable movements. Robin Uthappa moved from Rajasthan Royals to Chennai Super Kings, while Harshal Patel and Daniel Sams joined Royal Challengers Bangalore from Delhi Capitals.The trading window ahead of the 2020 season featured several player movements across franchises. Mumbai Indians brought in Sherfane Rutherford from Delhi Capitals and Dhawal Kulkarni from Rajasthan Royals, while Mayank Markande moved from Mumbai to Delhi before joining Rajasthan.Mumbai Indians strengthened their squad with two transfers announced ahead of the 2019 season, bringing in Quinton de Kock from Royal Challengers Bangalore and Jayant Yadav from Delhi Capitals.Rising Pune Supergiant made two notable acquisitions ahead of the 2017 season, bringing in Mayank Agarwal from Delhi Daredevils and Shardul Thakur from Kings XI Punjab.RCB acquired Iqbal Abdulla from Rajasthan Royals, Manvinder Bisla from Kolkata Knight Riders and Mandeep Singh from Kings XI Punjab. Mumbai brought in Parthiv Patel from Bangalore, Unmukt Chand from Rajasthan and R Vinay Kumar from Kolkata.The Ross Taylor-Ashish Nehra exchange was the standout transaction ahead of the 2013 season. Taylor moved from Delhi Daredevils to Pune Warriors India, while Nehra travelled in the opposite direction.Dinesh Karthik moved from Kings XI Punjab to Mumbai Indians, while Rajagopal Sathish went the other way. Former England cricketer and match referee Chris Broad has launched a scathing attack on former Australia head coach Darren Lehmann over the 2018 ball-tampering scandal, questioning how he could have been unaware of the incident and arguing that he escaped accountability.Broad's comments come amid fresh revelations by former Australia batter Usman Khawaja , who has claimed in his upcoming autobiography, Sabr, that the entire Australian squad, including players and support staff, knew about the ball-tampering episode during the tour of South Africa.Taking aim at Lehmann, who was Australia's head coach at the time, Broad questioned how he could have remained unaware of what was happening within the dressing room.""Darren Lehmann surely knew all about it,"" Broad said on Track Radio, as quoted by Fox Sports. ""And if he did not, he should not have been the coach at the time. I think he has got away lightly … OK, he left his job a few months later, but he did not get any sanctions.""The former England player also brought up Lehmann's criticism of his son, former England fast bowler Stuart Broad, during the 2013 Ashes series.Stuart had refused to walk after edging a delivery to the slips, prompting Lehmann to publicly criticise him.The then Australia coach subsequently warned that his side would make the England pacer ""cry"" when they toured Australia.Drawing a contrast with Lehmann's conduct during the 2018 scandal, Chris Broad questioned how the former coach could have denied knowledge of the incident.""And here he is, the coach of the Australian cricket team that brought sandpaper out onto the field of play and denied any knowledge of this happening. I am very angry at Darren Lehmann in this respect,"" Broad said.The controversy erupted during the third Test against South Africa in Cape Town in March 2018, when Cameron Bancroft was caught attempting to alter the condition of the ball using sandpaper. Then captain Steve Smith and vice-captain David Warner were handed one-year bans from competitive cricket, while Bancroft received a nine-month suspension from international and domestic cricket.Khawaja has argued that the responsibility for the episode was collective and that Smith, Warner and Bancroft should not have been left to shoulder the blame alone. He also questioned Cricket Australia's investigation, claiming that several members of the team were not interviewed despite allegedly having knowledge of the incident.In his autobiography, Khawaja further alleged that Australia had used sandpaper during the second Test in Gqeberha, before the episode came to light in Cape Town. He also made claims about attempts to alter the ball during the 2017-18 home Ashes series, alleging that players had lifted the quarter-seam to facilitate reverse swing.Australia won the third Test in Perth by an innings, a victory that helped them regain the Ashes.Broad's criticism has also received unexpected support from former Australia opener David Warner, who was among the players handed a one-year ban following the Cape Town scandal.""I could not agree more, and that's hard for me to say!"" The Indian Olympic Association's (IOA) presidential race took an unexpected turn on Monday, with current chief PT Usha facing her biggest electoral setback since taking charge of the organisation in December 2022.Usha, who became the first woman to head the IOA, finished fifth in the election for the women's Sportspersons of Outstanding Merit (SOM) category on November 9. With four positions available, she missed out on a place in the newly elected group that will form part of the IOA General Assembly, dealing a significant blow to her prospects of securing another term.The result has also altered the power dynamics within the country's apex sports body ahead of the December 5 Executive Council elections, which will determine who leads Indian Olympic administration for the next four years.However, Usha's electoral defeat does not, by itself, settle the question of her future. The IOA Constitution, ratified on September 8, and the Election Bye-Laws provide a framework that leaves some room for an alternative route. Whether that route is available to Usha, and whether she intends to pursue it, are now central questions.Usha was elected unopposed as IOA president on December 10, 2022, after securing a place among the Sportspersons of Outstanding Merit.The SOM category has traditionally provided a route for accomplished sportspersons to enter the IOA General Assembly and subsequently contest elections to the Executive Council.The latest election, however, did not go her way.In the six-way contest for four women's SOM positions, long jumper Anju Bobby George topped the poll with 53 votes, followed by former India women's hockey captain Rani Rampal (50), former archer Dola Banerjee (45) and badminton player Saina Nehwal (43). Usha secured 40 votes, finishing behind Saina, while former basketball player Anitha Pauldurai received six.The four men's positions had already been filled unopposed by Olympic medallists Gagan Narang, Yogeshwar Dutt and Vijender Singh, along with former table tennis player Kamlesh Mehta.The eight elected SOMs will form part of the General Assembly and will be eligible to vote in the December 5 elections. One male and one female representative from this category will also be elected to the Executive Council.For Usha, the immediate consequence is that she will no longer have the SOM route that helped her enter the IOA's electoral structure in 2022.But does that automatically rule her out of the presidential race? Not necessarily.The IOA Constitution provides for membership of the General Assembly through multiple categories, including representatives of National Sports Federations (NSFs), the Athletes Commission, IOC members and the eight SOMs.Under the election notification issued on November 9, each eligible NSF has been asked to nominate two authorised representatives to the Electoral College — one male and one female.The notification lists 30 eligible National Sports Federations. Each federation's representatives will have one vote apiece in the Executive Council elections.This potentially offers Usha an alternative route into the General Assembly, provided a federation nominates her as one of its authorised representatives and she meets the prescribed eligibility conditions.There are, however, important qualifications.The notification makes it clear that an authorised representative must be a member of the concerned NSF, an Indian citizen, below 70 years of age and in good standing. The nomination must also be supported by the federation's authorisation and submitted within the stipulated deadline.Therefore, Usha cannot simply secure a nomination from any federation without meeting its membership requirements.The Athletics Federation of India (AFI) is an obvious organisation to watch in this context, given Usha's association with athletics. However, there is no confirmed indication that she will be among its two representatives.More importantly, entering the General Assembly and satisfying the specific eligibility requirements for the post of president are two related but distinct considerations.The new Constitution's eligibility provision for the President and Treasurer requires a candidate to be a Sportsperson of Outstanding Merit or to have previously served at least one full term as a member of the IOA Executive Council, or as president, secretary general or treasurer of an affiliated unit.Usha's tenure as IOA president began in December 2022. Whether her current Executive Council service will be treated as a completed full term at the relevant eligibility cut-off is a question that will need to be assessed under the Constitution and by the Electoral Officer.The Constitution also provides for a four-year term for office-bearers, a three-term ceiling and a cooling-off provision in the circumstances specified under its tenure rules.Thus, while an NSF nomination could potentially restore her place in the General Assembly, it should not be viewed as an automatic clearance for the presidential contest.There is another significant development.According to reports, PT Usha is not currently considering seeking nomination from an NSF to regain entry into the General Assembly. Nor is she contemplating approaching the courts to challenge the SOM election result. Instead, her immediate focus appears to be on seeking intervention from the International Olympic Committee (IOC).In a confidential three-page complaint, addressed to IOC president Kirsty Coventry, Usha has sought an independent examination of the SOM election process.The complaint, accessed by TOI , raises concerns about alleged campaigning by incumbent Executive Council members, communications seeking confirmation of voters' participation and references to the Sports Ministry in messages concerning a secret-ballot election.Usha has also questioned the handling of four representations she claims to have submitted to Returning Officer Sanjay K. Srivastava during the electoral process.She has argued that the issue is not simply about her defeat, but about the conduct and oversight of the election itself.Her complaint reportedly asks the IOC to examine the alleged violations, ascertain whether any government or external influence was exerted and consider referring the matter to its relevant ethics and compliance mechanisms.She has also sought corrective measures to safeguard future IOA elections.The letter comes against the backdrop of India's ambitions to host the 2036 Olympic Games. Usha has argued that the IOA's independence, transparency and governance standards are important to the credibility of the Olympic movement.Sources in her camp have indicated that the immediate hope is for IOC intervention, alongside efforts to seek the Prime Minister's Office's intervention into the alleged irregularities.With the SOM elections concluded, the IOA has moved to the next phase of its Executive Council election process. Electoral Officer Sanjay K. Srivastava has formally announced December 5 as the date for the Executive Council elections.The immediate task is to constitute the Electoral College, which will elect the next president and other office-bearers.Under the notification, the 30 eligible NSFs have been asked to submit the names of their two authorised representatives between November 10 and November 12, by 3 pm.The provisional Electoral College is scheduled to be published on November 12. Objections can be submitted until 6 pm on November 13, followed by scrutiny and disposal of objections on November 14. The final Electoral Roll is scheduled for publication on November 15.The Electoral College will comprise:- Two authorised representatives from each of the 30 eligible National Sports Federations.- IOC member(s), each entitled to one vote.- Two representatives of the IOA Athletes Commission.- Eight elected Sportspersons of Outstanding Merit, comprising four men and four women.The eight SOMs, therefore, will have a role beyond simply occupying positions in the General Assembly. They will also be part of the body that elects the next IOA leadership.","PT Usha has been the IOA president since December 2022. Former India cricketer Ajay Jadeja has praised Arshdeep Singh's overall performance in India's five-wicket victory over New Zealand in the first ODI in Auckland, but believes the left-arm pacer could have avoided an expensive finish to his spell.India began their five-match ODI series with a comfortable win at Eden Park on Wednesday, November 4. Virat Kohli led the chase with a fluent 74, while Shubman Gill contributed 37 as the duo stitched together a 113-run partnership. India eventually crossed the finish line with five wickets to spare and 56 deliveries remaining.With the ball, Arshdeep was India's leading wicket-taker, claiming four wickets in his 10 overs. However, his figures of 4/70 were inflated by an expensive final over in which New Zealand tailender Blair Tickner struck him for three sixes, taking 23 runs off the over.Assessing the pacer's performance, Jadeja felt Arshdeep had been impressive for most of his spell but allowed the opportunity to complete a five-wicket haul to influence his bowling towards the end.""I would call him slightly greedy. From 14 medals in 2010 to 114 in 2026, India’s remarkable rise continued in Aichi-Nagoya as a smaller contingent surpassed its previous best, achieved 30 gold medals and secured its highest-ever finish at the continental para-sport showpiece.India’s campaign at the Asian Para Games 2026 was a triumph that few would have predicted when the size of the contingent became known. With just 167 athletes travelling to Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, the prospect of repeating the 100-plus medal haul achieved at Hangzhou in 2023 appeared ambitious. The previous edition had seen India send more than 300 athletes to the competition, returning with a record 108 medals after subsequent revisions to the original tally.But the Indian contingent defied expectations, producing an even bigger return with significantly fewer athletes. India finished the fifth edition of the Asian Para Games with 114 medals — 30 gold, 35 silver and 49 bronze — to secure fourth place, both the highest medal tally and the best finish in the country's history at the event.The numbers tell a compelling story of progress. India improved its medal tally for the fifth consecutive edition, added to its gold-medal record and finished ahead of South Korea, which had threatened to challenge its position in the final standings.More than the record itself, the achievement highlighted how far India's para-sport movement has travelled in 16 years — from a modest 14-medal return at the inaugural edition in 2010 to a fourth-place finish among Asia's leading para-sport nations.India's progress at the Asian Para Games has been steady, with each edition bringing a new high in the overall medal tally.At Guangzhou in 2010, India won 14 medals — one gold, four silver and nine bronze — to finish 15th. The 2014 edition in Incheon brought a substantial improvement, with the country collecting 33 medals, including three gold, but remaining 15th in the standings.The breakthrough arrived at Jakarta in 2018. India's medal tally rose to 72, comprising 15 gold, 24 silver and 33 bronze, while its position improved to ninth.Hangzhou in 2023 marked another major leap. India crossed the 100-medal barrier for the first time, initially returning with 111 medals before the tally was revised to 108 following a doping-related disqualification and a medal reallocation. The revised haul comprised 27 gold, 32 silver and 49 bronze, with India eventually classified sixth.Aichi-Nagoya extended that upward trajectory. India added six medals to its revised Hangzhou total, increased its gold-medal count from 27 to 30 and climbed two places to fourth.The numbers at a glance: India's medal tally increased more than eightfold between 2010 and 2026. Its gold-medal count grew from one to 30, while its position improved from 15th to fourth.The rise has not been limited to the overall tally. India has improved its standing in three successive editions since 2014, moving from 15th to ninth, then sixth and now fourth. The 2026 result represents the culmination of a sustained upward trend rather than an isolated breakthrough.The most striking feature of India's latest performance was the efficiency with which its athletes converted participation into medals.India fielded 167 athletes — 111 men and 56 women — across 11 sports at Aichi-Nagoya. That was considerably fewer than the 309 athletes listed for the Hangzhou campaign in 2023, yet the team surpassed its previous best by six medals.The comparison is revealing. India sent approximately 46 per cent fewer athletes than it did to Hangzhou, but its medal tally increased by nearly six per cent. The gold-medal count rose by three, the silver tally by three, and the bronze count remained unchanged.On a simple medals-per-athlete measure, India's return increased from approximately 0.35 medals per athlete in Hangzhou to 0.68 in Aichi-Nagoya. This is an aggregate comparison, not an individual success rate, since athletes can win multiple medals and the number of events and opportunities varies across sports.Nevertheless, the figures underline the scale of the achievement. A smaller squad did not merely match the previous edition's success
column2: it established a new benchmark for Indian para-sport.Para-athletics was the backbone of India's campaign, delivering 65 medals — 22 gold, 19 silver and 24 bronze. That represented nearly 57 per cent of the country's overall tally and made athletics the single biggest contributor to India's fourth-place finish.Para-badminton followed with 16 medals, including three gold, five silver and eight bronze. Together, athletics and badminton accounted for 81 medals, more than 70 per cent of India's total.Swimming contributed 11 medals, comprising three silver and eight bronze. Archery added six medals, including three gold and three silver, while shooting produced five, with two gold, two silver and one bronze.Athletics' contribution also illustrates how India's progress has accelerated. At Hangzhou, para-athletics produced 52 medals, including 16 gold, 17 silver and 19 bronze. In Aichi-Nagoya, the discipline's haul rose to 65, with six additional gold medals.Badminton's contribution was different. India won 21 medals in the sport at Hangzhou, including four gold, but finished with 16 in 2026. Instead, the substantial gains in athletics and the contributions from other sports helped compensate for the decline in badminton medals.That distinction matters: the record haul reflects both the strength of India's established medal-winning disciplines and the need to broaden its success across events in future editions.India's record was supported by athletes who delivered more than once during the competition. A total of 26 Indian athletes won multiple medals, while six athletes collected multiple gold medals, demonstrating the importance of individual excellence in a campaign involving 11 sports.Archer Sheetal Devi was among the standout performers, winning two gold medals and a silver. Her two golds came in the mixed compound and individual compound events, while the silver added to her three-medal haul.Athletics provided several other multiple gold medallists. Dilip Gavit, Nishad Kumar, Pranav Soorma and Simran Sharma each won two gold medals, while shooting contributed through Mona Agarwal, who also secured two golds.Four athletes finished with three medals apiece: Sheetal Devi in archery, Thulasimathi Murugesan in badminton, Ravi Budigina in swimming and Himanshu Nandal in swimming. Their performances illustrated how athletes winning across multiple events can make a significant difference to a country's final tally.The figures also invite comparison with Hangzhou, where 25 Indian athletes won multiple medals. The increase to 26 in 2026 was modest, but the overall tally improved despite a much smaller contingent. The result points to a campaign in which medal-winning performances were concentrated among a relatively small squad.India's rise at the Asian Para Games has coincided with a significant improvement at the Paralympics, strengthening the country's standing in international para-sport.At Rio 2016, India won four medals and finished 43rd. Tokyo 2020 marked a breakthrough, with 19 medals — five gold, eight silver and six bronze — lifting India to 24th. At Paris 2024, India recorded its best Paralympic haul of 29 medals, comprising seven gold, nine silver and 13 bronze, to finish 18th.The progression at the Paralympics mirrors the broader trend at the Asian Para Games: larger medal returns, more gold medals and improvements in the standings.India's able-bodied contingent had also finished fourth at the 2026 Asian Games, although its 85-medal tally was below the 106 medals achieved at Hangzhou in 2023. The para contingent's performance offered a contrasting story of growth, with its medal count rising and its position improving.China dominated Aichi-Nagoya, finishing with 435 medals, including 207 gold. Hosts Japan were second with 186 medals, while Uzbekistan finished third with 145. India placed fourth with 114, ahead of South Korea, which collected 100 medals, including 29 gold.India's final position was not guaranteed until the closing stages. South Korea remained within reach, but its final-day return of one gold and two silver left it one gold behind India. The Indian contingent held on to fourth place with 30 gold, 35 silver and 49 bronze.The gap to third-placed Uzbekistan shows that further progress will require India to expand its medal-winning strength across disciplines. Yet the immediate achievement is significant: India has moved from 15th at the first two editions to fourth, while increasing its tally at every successive Games.The challenge now is to sustain that momentum, build a deeper pool of competitive athletes and reduce dependence on a handful of disciplines.For a contingent of just 167 athletes, 114 medals represent more than a record. They mark the latest step in a 16-year transformation of Indian para-sport — one that began with 14 medals in Guangzhou and has now culminated in a historic fourth-place finish in Aichi-Nagoya.","India fielded 167 athletes — 111 men and 56 women — across 11 sports at Aichi- Nagoya. NEW DELHI: Suhas Yathiraj was disappointed with his bronze medal at the Asian Para Games in Nagoya. Having beaten Indonesia's Fredy Setiawan in their group match just days earlier, the Indian shuttler had hoped to reach the final and fight for gold.Suhas lost the men's singles SL4 semifinal 23-21, 8-21, 15-21. He had chances to take the opening game but failed to convert them. After bouncing back to win the second game 21-8, he lost focus at a crucial stage of the decider.“Definitely not satisfied with bronze. I think if I had played up to my full potential, I would have definitely done better. In fact, I defeated Fredy of Indonesia in the group match in Nagoya only a few days ago,” Suhas told TimesofIndia.com from Aichi-Nagoya in Japan.“In the semifinal match, the first set was very close. I lost 23-21 and I had game point, set point, but I couldn't convert that. In the second set, I won very easily. In the third set, I think after 10-all, I sort of lost focus for two to three rallies. That is where he took the game. So, it was not my best day, I would assume. I would always love to win a gold medal. So, yes, I am a little sad from that angle,” he said.The defeat also reminded him of how important it is to perform under pressure at major tournaments.“It is the most important factor to win medals at major games because you might be training well, you might actually have the fitness and the skills. But if you don't recreate that during the major games, then probably it is of not much use in terms of professional success,” Suhas said.Suhas, an IAS officer, said he had never imagined representing India in international badminton a decade ago.In November 2016, he made his debut at the Asian Championships in Beijing and won gold. Since then, he has won several medals at major international events. These include bronze at the 2018 Asian Para Games in Jakarta, silver at the Tokyo 2020 Paralympics, another silver at the Paris 2024 Paralympics, gold at the Hangzhou Asian Para Games and bronze in Nagoya.The 43-year-old has represented India at two Paralympic Games, Tokyo in 2020 and Paris in 2024, winning silver on both occasions.With the Los Angeles 2028 Paralympics approaching, the big question is whether he can go one step further and win gold.The desire is there, but Suhas is not looking too far ahead. He wants to take things one step at a time.“If you had asked me 10 years ago, I didn't even know that I would play for India. But whenever I look at the medals and the love I have got from fans and sportspersons around the world, the journey has been quite satisfying. I have had the honour of wearing the Indian jersey and winning medals for my country,” he said.“I am grateful for what God has given me. I never imagined that I would become an IAS officer one day, an Arjuna awardee or a badminton player winning medals for India. I never imagined all this. But thanks to the Almighty for all these,” Suhas, who is also an Arjuna Award recipient, said.“So if God and destiny have been kind to me, I hope they will take me to a place that I deserve. I hope I can do the best that I can in whatever I choose to,” he added.For most people, the end of a hectic working day is a time to relax, spend time with family, play with their children or watch a movie.For Suhas, it is often time to pick up his badminton racket and head to the court. His day includes early-morning gym sessions, office work, inspections, meetings, video conferences and checking files. Despite his demanding responsibilities as an IAS officer, he makes time for badminton and follows a strict fitness routine to compete at the highest level.Balancing the two careers is not easy, but his love for the sport keeps him going.“If you choose what you love, then the journey becomes painless. You enjoy that journey. That's what I do,” Suhas said.Explaining how he manages his work and training, he said: “It is challenging. My training generally starts in the night and it always involves sacrifices. Probably others would be spending time with their family members or having leisure time. My leisure time is to play badminton. In badminton, you need an extremely high level of fitness. It's challenging, hectic but at the same time I love it.”“I don't remember eating sweets in the last many months. I can't recall when I had my last sweet. So, I almost don't eat sweets or fried food and am also quite conscious about the nutrition that I take,” he said.Suhas grew up watching Malaysian badminton great Lee Chong Wei and was inspired by his movement on the court.“Yes, I have always been inspired by so many top players in the able-bodied category. Growing up, I watched the matches of Lee Chong Wei and how he used to move around the court,” he said.“Even in India, the top shuttlers perform extremely well, whether it is Lakshya Sen, HS Prannoy or Kidambi Srikanth. I know them personally and have always admired how well they are able to compete at the top,” Suhas signed off.","Suhas Yathiraj was disappointed with his bronze medal at the Asian Para Games in Nagoya. NEW DELHI: India signed off from the Aichi-Nagoya 2026 Asian Para Games with their best-ever medal haul of 114 medals as the week-long continental competition concluded with a closing ceremony at the Mizuho Park Athletics Stadium in Nagoya, Japan, on Saturday.Double gold medallists Nishad Kumar and Mona Agarwal led the Indian contingent as flag-bearers at the ceremony, marking the end of a landmark campaign in which the country's para-athletes delivered historic victories, world-record performances and podium sweeps across disciplines.India finished fourth in the overall standings with 30 gold, 35 silver and 49 bronze medals, surpassing its previous best of 108 medals at the 2022 Hangzhou Games.Held in Japan for the first time, the fifth edition of the Asian Para Games brought together around 4,000 athletes and staff from 45 countries and regions. She also extended her congratulations to the entire Indian contingent.Para athletics was India's biggest medal contributor, accounting for 65 medals — 22 gold, 19 silver and 24 bronze. The contingent added two medals each in para judo and para powerlifting.The closing ceremony brought together athletes, officials and dignitaries to mark the conclusion of the Games. Asian Paralympic Committee president Majid Rashed declared the event closed, highlighting the growing strength of para sport across Asia and its role in building a more inclusive society.Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi also praised the athletes' determination, teamwork and sportsmanship, describing their performances as a reminder of the “profound beauty” of para sports.The Asian Para Games began in Guangzhou, China, in 2010, evolving from the Far East and South Pacific Games Federation for the Disabled. Albert Einstein showed beyond doubt that time wasn’t absolute, as Isaac Newton believed – trust a former German citizen to ruin an Englishman’s conception of the universe – but for now, without access to vehicles that move at the speed of light, the absolute and linear concept of time is the only human experience that exists without taking psychedelic substances. And sadly, that means slowly, the greats who have defined the last two decades of sports are slowly being put out to pasture in retirement. In tennis, Roger Federer and Rafael Nadal – two gentlemen who redefined both the game and the art of being gentlemen – have hung up their rackets. We will never see their contrasting games – Renaissance painter with a racket vs a Davidian sculpture made with a chisel – ever come up against one another. The same goes for football, where Lionel Messi and Cristiano Ronaldo have now both hung up their international footballing boots.Both careers played out in the Age of Social Media, and much has been written – even in Offside – about Ronaldo’s insouciant petulance in the last days of his career, but remembrances should be about good things, not bad ones.In earlier editions of Offside, we have argued that Portugal needed to put its GOAT out to pasture , written about Spain handing Ronaldo a reality check , and lamented how watching Ronaldo had become painful, even for a Ronaldo fan . This time, we will remember the happiness he gave us.For once, let’s stop being captivated by the carousel of constant negativity and remember what the boy from Madeira – that’s closer to Morocco than Lisbon – meant to Portugal as a player.Now, much has been written about his numbers. Ronaldo has scored in six World Cups and five Euros, and has scored in 23 consecutive years. Of Portugal’s total goals at major tournaments, he has scored 19.2 per cent. There’s a very clear Portugal before Ronaldo, which, despite the likes of Luis Figo and Co, barely made a dent in tournaments, and a Portugal after Ronaldo, which looked like a team of substance.It’s also unlikely – unless Romelu Lukaku or Harry Kane go on Ronaldo-like scoring sprees – that anyone will beat his record of 146 international goals. But football isn’t about numbers: little kids don’t dream of xGs but of how the beautiful game makes us feel.There are moments in the Ronaldo highlight reel where fans and the wider footballing public were drawn in by the remarkable drama that followed.Like Euro 2004 – the same year his future Manchester United wingman and footballing soulmate Wayne Rooney burst onto the stage – when Ronaldo wept after losing to Greece in the final. Or the World Cup two years later, when Ronaldo winked at his bench after ensuring Rooney got sent off for playing with a different set of balls – before dispatching the penalty that knocked England out of the World Cup. He would come back as Public Enemy Number 1 in the UK, something that the wily Sir Alex Ferguson used to his advantage to forge the world-beating generation of Ronaldo and Co, including the 2008 Ballon d’Or that fans voted the greatest Ballon d’Or of all time.Or when he sat heartbroken – a moth fluttering over his nose after he got injured – as Portugal somehow pulled through to beat France in the Euro 2016 final that became as famous for Ronaldo’s managerial theatrics as it did for Portugal’s first major trophy. And then, while going to collect the trophy, he spotted Sir Alex, who hugged him like a Biblical prodigal son returning home.Or the 2014 World Cup qualifier showdown between Ronaldo and Zlatan – when Portugal met Sweden – which saw Ronaldo drag Portugal into the World Cup by sheer willpower.Then there was 2018, when one hat-trick appeared to cause a glitch in David de Gea’s goalkeeping algorithm – before that he was impossible to beat, and afterwards he kept getting beaten like Onana – in which Portugal drew 3-3 with Spain.The man named after Ronald Reagan would turn up for his nation whenever required, scoring when everything looked lost, and would add two UEFA Nations League titles. Yes, his tantrums would be panned on social media
column2: at times, his overall global fame perhaps became detrimental and overshadowed the Portuguese national team’s fortunes.But there’s no doubt that because of Cristiano Ronaldo, Portugal became the team to watch and support for millions of fans across the globe.When Ronaldo first played for Portugal in August 2003, he came on as a substitute for Luís Figo, the man who was then the country's greatest footballing superstar. Ronaldo would eventually inherit Figo's No. 7 shirt, a number already associated with Portuguese footballing greatness.While Figo crossed the Barcelona-Madrid divide and got a pig’s head thrown at him for his lack of loyalty, Ronaldo, after winning everything with Manchester United, became the world’s most expensive footballer when he joined Real Madrid, which seems like a bargain at GBP 80 million, making him slightly cheaper than what Manchester United paid for Antony. During his time in Madrid, he won four Champions Leagues and well surpassed Figo’s record there. His shirt became one of the most recognised in the world.In his retirement announcement, Ronaldo spoke about handing back the No. 7 shirt, which he had worn for 23 years. It was a rather poignant admission from a man who had spent much of his career appearing almost invincible. The shirt that once belonged to Figo, and then became synonymous with Ronaldo, will now belong to someone else.When Ronaldo inherited Figo’s shirt, an entire generation of football fans was still growing up. Those same fans are now adults, many with children of their own, who have spent their lives watching Ronaldo defy age, expectations and occasionally common sense. For them, his retirement also marks the end of a part of their own lives.There will be other great Portuguese footballers, other No. 7s and perhaps even someone who breaks Ronaldo's extraordinary records. But the next player to wear that shirt will inherit an enormous burden of expectations.The No. 7 shirt has become something of a poisoned chalice at Manchester United since Ronaldo left for Madrid, and it proved to be a burden even for Ronaldo himself when he returned. Hopefully, it won’t become an albatross for the next Portuguese player who puts it on.Ronaldo’s footballing legacy will outlast the goals he has scored, the appearances he has made and the trophies he has won with club and country. Go to any corner of the world and you’ll find some random kid leaping into the air and copying his celebration. And that is something no statistic can measure. Einstein showed us that time isn’t absolute. We still don’t have a time machine or a way to travel at anything close to the speed of light. But watch those old Ronaldo highlights from our youth, and for a few fleeting moments, the years seem to disappear. We are young again, watching the man who gave us so much happiness.
